How, then, had she managed—she who was so intelligent!—to be mistaken yet again? Besides, through what deplorable mania had she thus ruined her life in continual sacrifices? She recalled all her instincts for luxury, all the privations of her soul, the baseness of marriage, of domestic life, her dreams falling into the mud like wounded swallows, everything she had desired, everything she had denied herself, everything she might have had! And why? Why?

Amid the silence that filled the village, a heartrending cry passed through the air. Bovary turned pale, almost fainting. She frowned with a nervous gesture, then continued. Yet it was for him, for that creature, for that man who understood nothing, who felt nothing! For there he was, perfectly calm, without even suspecting that the ridiculousness of his name would henceforth soil her as it did him. She had made efforts to love him, and she had repented with tears for having yielded to another.

“But perhaps it was a valgus!” Bovary suddenly exclaimed, deep in thought.

At the unexpected impact of this sentence, dropping onto her thoughts like a lead ball onto a silver platter, Emma started and raised her head to guess what he meant; and they looked at each other in silence, almost astonished to see one another, so far apart were they in their consciousness. Charles regarded her with the clouded gaze of a drunken man, while listening motionlessly to the amputee’s final cries, which followed one another in drawn-out modulations, broken by sharp jolts, like the distant howling of some animal being slaughtered. Emma bit her pale lips and, rolling between her fingers one of the branches of the coral she had broken, fixed upon Charles the burning tips of her eyes, like two fiery arrows ready to fly. Everything about him irritated her now: his face, his clothes, what he did not say, his entire person, his very existence. She repented of her former virtue as though it were a crime, and what still remained of it was crumbling beneath the furious blows of her pride. She reveled in all the malicious ironies of triumphant adultery. The memory of her lover returned to her with dizzying allurements: she cast her soul into it, swept toward that image by a new enthusiasm; and Charles seemed to her as detached from her life, as forever absent, as impossible and annihilated, as if he were about to die and had lain in his death agony before her eyes.

There came a sound of footsteps on the pavement. Charles looked; and through the lowered blind he saw, at the edge of the market halls, in full sunlight, Doctor Canivet wiping his forehead with his handkerchief. Homais, behind him, carried a large red box in his hand, and they were both making their way toward the pharmacy.

Then, out of sudden tenderness and discouragement, Charles turned to his wife and said to her:

“Do kiss me, my dear!”

“Leave me alone!” she said, her face crimson with anger.

“What is it? What is it?” he repeated, dumbfounded. “Calm down! Pull yourself together!... You know very well that I love you!... Come!”

“Enough!” she cried with a terrible expression.

And, fleeing from the room, Emma slammed the door so hard that the barometer leapt from the wall and shattered on the floor.

Charles collapsed into his armchair, distraught, trying to determine what might be wrong with her, imagining some nervous illness, weeping, and vaguely sensing something ominous and incomprehensible moving around him.

When Rodolphe arrived in the garden that evening, he found his mistress waiting for him at the foot of the front steps, on the first step. They embraced, and all their resentment melted like snow beneath the warmth of that kiss.

XII

They began to love each other again. Often, even in the middle of the day, Emma would suddenly write to him; then, through the windowpanes, she would signal to Justin, who, quickly untying his floor cloth, would fly off to La Huchette. Rodolphe would arrive; it was so that she could tell him that she was bored, that her husband was odious and her life dreadful!

“Can I do anything about it?” he exclaimed one day, growing impatient.

“Ah! If only you were willing!...”

She was sitting on the floor between his knees, her hair loosened at the sides, her gaze lost.

“What, then?” said Rodolphe.

She sighed.

“We would go and live elsewhere... somewhere...”

“You really are mad!” he said, laughing. “Is that possible?”

She returned to the subject; he pretended not to understand and changed the conversation.

What he did not understand was all this turmoil over something as simple as love. She had a motive, a reason, and something like an ally supporting her attachment.

Indeed, this tenderness grew greater every day under the influence of her revulsion for her husband. The more she gave herself to the one, the more she abhorred the other; never did Charles seem so disagreeable to her, his fingers so square, his mind so dull, his manners so common, as after her meetings with Rodolphe, when they were together. Then, while playing the wife and the virtuous woman, she would take fire at the thought of that head whose black hair curled toward the tanned forehead, of that figure at once so robust and so elegant, of that man, in short, who possessed so much experience in reason, so much passion in desire! It was for him that she filed her nails with an engraver’s care, and that there could never be enough cold cream on her skin or patchouli in her handkerchiefs. She loaded herself with bracelets, rings, necklaces. When he was due to come, she filled her two large blue glass vases with roses, and arranged her apartment and her person like a courtesan awaiting a prince. The maid had to be constantly laundering linen; and all day long Félicité never left the kitchen, where young Justin, who often kept her company, watched her work.

With his elbow on the long board where she ironed, he gazed avidly at all those women’s things spread out around him: the dimity petticoats, the fichus, the little collars, and the drawstring drawers, broad at the hips and narrowing toward the bottom.
